newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Shots in Kinshasa, firing in Zaire's 2nd city.
newsitem.headline: Shots in Kinshasa, firing in Zaire's 2nd city.

text.p: Shots rang out in Zaire's capital Kinshasa on Wednesday as security forces tried to break up a march by thousands of supporters of new prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi, witnesses said.

In southern Zaire, intense gunfire and mortar bomb explosions broke out in the suburbs of Lubumbashi, as Laurent Kabila's rebel forces closed in on the sprawling country's second city, witnesses said.

In Kinshasa, security forces were battling Tshisekedi supporters who turned out to accompany the veteran opposition leader and foe of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko to the prime minister's offices where he planned to install himself with his team.

Witnesses reported shooting after the crowd broke through a cordon of security forces who were blocking the approaches to the prime minister's offices a day after Mobutu declared a state of emergency.
Tshisekedi himself, tears streaming down his face from the teargas, walked in the direction of the offices. Armoured vehicles blocked the way further down the road.
One unconfirmed report said that Tshisekedi had been slightly injured.
Earlier, members of the feared civil guard turned on Tshisekedi sympathisers and journalists near his home, hitting them with rifle butts.
"The new state of emergency is for the dustbin. Mobutu made the decision all alone," Tshisekedi's minister of posts and telecommunications, Modeste Kikunga, told Reuters.
He said members of the new government planned to regroup and try again to move into the prime minister's offices.
Thousands of Tshisekedi supporters, many waving branches and leaves, gathered on the November 24 roundabout and avenue in the city centre.
Mobutu's son Kongolo, a member of the presidential guard and known locally as Saddam Hussein, was with senior army commanders barring access to the prime minister's offices, witnesses said.
But Tshisekedi officials said they were confident that the security forces would allow Tshisekedi himself through.

In Lubumbashi, Reuters correspondent Richard Meares said the fighting was in the southern suburbs of the city and wild shouts of joy could be heard from crowds less than one km (half a mile) from his hotel, along with chants of "Kabila, Kabila".
Hours earlier, residents of Lubumbashi reported that people had fled the city centre which was now deserted. Government soldiers were commandeering vehicles in the city, they said.

Kabila, whose forces have seized nearly half the country since taking up arms in October, said on Tuesday that members of Mobutu's elite presidential guard were putting up a fight on the approaches to Lubumbashi which is near the Zambian border.

In Lusaka, Foreign Minister Lawrence Shimba said on Wednesday Zambia would not allow anyone to use its territory to launch attacks on Zaire. He was responding to Zambian press reports that opponents of Mobutu who had been living in Zambia as refugees had returned home to join the rebels.
In Geneva, a U.N. spokesman said its Zaire envoy expected a truce in "a matter of days" at peace talks in South Africa.
Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 but has seen his hold over country crumble as the rebels advance, announced the state of emergency via a decree read on state television late on Tuesday.

He appointed military governors to Kinshasa and other areas not under rebel control. His decree did not make clear what restrictions would be imposed or the implications for Kinshasa and its more than five million people.
Tshisekedi is under fire from Mobutu supporters and allies alike after less than a week in the job and announcing a government composed only of his most loyal followers.
He earmaked six posts for the rebels, who took up arms in October vowing to topple Mobutu and who hold nearly half of the country, but the offer was rebuffed.
Kabila, speaking in Mbuji-Mayi, the capital of Tshisekedi's diamond-rich home province of Kasai on Tuesday, said the new prime minister and his supporters should make a complete break with Mobutu.
"The real problem with Tshisekedi is that Mobutu is always in the background, manoeuvring to divide the opposition and remain always in control," said Kabila.

Outgoing prime minister Kengo wa Dondo and his team have said Tshisekedi's government has not formally taken power as it has not won the blessing of parliament. The assembly voted out Kengo following persistent charges that he mismanaged the war.
